content: Drospirenone is a synthetic progestin that is structurally and pharmacologically analogous to spironolactone. Its molecular formula is C24H30O3. This compound is utilized in certain oral contraceptive formulations. Drospirenone distinguishes itself from other synthetic progestins due to its pharmacological profile, which closely resembles that of natural progesterone, as demonstrated in preclinical studies. It exhibits anti-mineralocorticoid properties, counteracts the estrogen-stimulated activity of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, and lacks androgenic effects. These characteristics, similar to those of spironolactone, may result in reduced water retention, decreased breast tenderness, and improved skin appearance, including a reduction in acne. When administered orally, drospirenone has a bioavailability of approximately 76%. It does not bind to sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG) or corticosteroid-binding globulin (CBG) but instead binds to other serum proteins. Its metabolites are not biologically active and are excreted primarily through urine and feces, with nearly complete elimination occurring within 10 days. Drospirenone is included in several newer oral contraceptive formulations. For example: Yasmin® contains 3 mg of drospirenone and 30 mcg of ethinyl estradiol per tablet. It is indicated for the prevention of pregnancy in women who choose to use oral contraceptives. Yaz® contains 3 mg of drospirenone and 20 mcg of ethinyl estradiol per tablet, administered in a 24/4-day regimen, with the same indications as Yasmin®. Another formulation includes 5 mg of drospirenone and 1 mg of estradiol per day, marketed as Angeliq®, which was introduced in the United States in 2007. Drospirenone has the potential to cause hyperkalemia in high-risk patients, with its effects being comparable to a 25 mg dose of spironolactone. It is contraindicated in patients with hepatic dysfunction, renal insufficiency, adrenal insufficiency, or in those for whom oral contraceptives are contraindicated, such as smokers and individuals with a history of deep vein thrombosis (DVT), stroke, or other thromboembolic events. Due to its anti-mineralocorticoid effects, caution is advised when drospirenone is used concurrently with other medications that may increase potassium levels. These include ACE inhibitors, angiotensin-II receptor antagonists, potassium-sparing diuretics, potassium supplements, heparin, aldosterone antagonists, and NSAIDs.
